client: I've been really stressed about things at home lately, and I guess that's why I finally decided to come in. My partner told me last week that they feel like I'm never really present anymore, and honestly, hearing that hit me harder than I expected. I'm not even sure talking about it will change anything, because the work pressure isn't going away anytime soon.
therapist: It sounds like your partner's words really landed somewhere deep — like they put into words something you'd been quietly carrying for a while. There's a lot of weight in what you're sharing, and I also notice a kind of resignation underneath it, almost like part of you wonders if anything can actually shift. I'm curious — when you imagine things being *different* at home, what would that even look like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I mean... when I try to picture it being different, I honestly don't even know what that looks like anymore. Like, I used to have this image of us actually talking at dinner, not just sitting there on our phones or going through the motions, but that feels so far away now that it almost seems naive to even want it. I guess part of me does wonder if it's too late, or if I've just... gotten used to feeling invisible in my own home.
therapist: That image of actually talking at dinner — that's not naive at all, that's you remembering what connection felt like, and it's still meaningful enough that you brought it up. I'm struck by the phrase "invisible in my own home," because that's such a lonely feeling, and it makes me wonder how long you've been carrying that without really naming it. What do you think started to shift — was there a moment, or did it feel more like a slow fade?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it was more of a slow fade, honestly. There wasn't one big fight or moment where everything changed — it just kind of... crept up on me, and one day I realized we were all just existing in the same space without really seeing each other. And the worst part is I'm not even sure anyone else in my family has noticed, which makes me feel like maybe I'm the problem somehow.
therapist: That leap — from "no one else has noticed" to "maybe I'm the problem" — is such a painful place to land, and it's worth slowing down there for a moment. It sounds like you're carrying a lot of quiet responsibility for something that likely grew from both sides of the relationship. What would it mean for you if it *wasn't* just your problem to fix?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... if it wasn't just my problem to fix, I guess that would feel like a relief, but honestly it's hard to actually believe that. Because if I'm not the one responsible, then I have no control over it either, and that almost feels worse in a way. Like at least if it's my fault, there's something I can do about it.
therapist: That's such a honest and insightful thing to recognize — that blame can actually feel safer than helplessness, because at least it gives you somewhere to put your energy. But I notice as you said it, there seemed to be something almost urgent underneath, like this idea of not being in control is genuinely frightening rather than just uncomfortable. What is it about losing that sense of control that feels so threatening to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I think... if I'm not in control, then I'm just waiting for something bad to happen and there's nothing I can do about it. Like, my friend group kind of fell apart over the past year, and I kept thinking if I had just said the right things or organized more hangouts, it wouldn't have happened. Letting go of that story means admitting I might just end up alone no matter what I do, and that's terrifying.
therapist: The fear underneath all of this is really coming through — that no matter how hard you try, connection might slip away anyway, and that's an incredibly vulnerable place to sit. What strikes me is that you've been working so hard to hold everything together, your friendships, your home life, almost like you've appointed yourself the guardian against loss. I'm wondering, has there ever been a time in your life where you felt secure in a relationship *without* having to manage it so carefully?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to say no, there's never been a time like that. But then I think about my grandmother, when I was really young, maybe eight or nine, I didn't have to do anything to earn her presence, she was just... there. The second I got older and started understanding that people leave, that people die, it's like I couldn't access that feeling anymore, and I've been scrambling ever since.
therapist: What you just described about your grandmother is so tender and important — that experience of being loved without having to earn it or maintain it is exactly what you've been searching for ever since, and it makes complete sense that losing her changed something fundamental in how safe connection felt. There's something almost bittersweet in the way you spoke about her, like that memory is both a comfort and a reminder of what you've been grieving for a long time. I'm curious — when you picture that little eight-year-old who could just *rest* in someone's presence, what do you think she most needs to hear right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know... when I think about her, that little girl, I just feel this wave of sadness because she had no idea what was coming, you know? Like she was so trusting and open, and then everything just kind of... closed up after my grandmother died. I guess what she needs to hear is that it's okay to still want that kind of closeness, but honestly, even saying that out loud feels a little naive, like I'm setting myself up to be hurt again.
therapist: You just gave that little girl something really important — you said out loud that it's okay to still want closeness, even if it felt scary to say. I notice you called it "naive," but I wonder if what you're really describing is courage — because wanting connection after you've been hurt by loss takes so much more bravery than closing off does. What would it feel like to hold onto that want, not as something that sets you up to fail, but as something that's actually been guiding you toward this room today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... when you put it that way, it does shift something a little. Like maybe wanting connection isn't just me setting myself up to get hurt again, but I'm not sure I fully believe that yet. It's easier to call it naive because then at least I feel like I'm being realistic, not just... hoping for something that keeps slipping away from me.
therapist: That distinction you just made — between "realistic" and "hoping" — is really worth sitting with, because somewhere along the way those two things became opposites for you, like hope itself became the dangerous thing. And it makes sense that "realistic" feels safer, because it's protected you, but I wonder if it's also cost you something. What would it mean to let "realistic" and "hopeful" exist at the same time, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe that's possible, but it feels almost contradictory in my head. Like if I let myself hope, I'm just setting myself up to be blindsided again, and being "realistic" is how I keep that from happening. I guess what it's cost me is... I don't know, maybe I've stopped letting myself want things, which sounds kind of sad when I say it out loud.
therapist: You said "that sounds kind of sad" almost like you were observing it from a distance, but I imagine it lands closer than that — because what you're really describing is years of quietly talking yourself out of wanting things you deeply deserve. That's not a small thing to recognize. What feels most present for you right now, sitting with that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I guess "sad" was kind of a safe word for it. When you put it that way — years of talking myself out of wanting things — it actually feels heavier than I expected, like there's this weight in my chest right now that I don't usually let myself notice. I think what's most present is this uncomfortable mix of recognizing it's true and immediately wanting to dismiss it again, because sitting with it feels almost dangerous somehow.
therapist: That weight in your chest — that's not something to dismiss, that's actually you making contact with something really real, maybe for the first time in a long time. The urge to pull away from it makes complete sense, because sitting with pain without immediately fixing it is unfamiliar territory when you've spent years in protection mode. I'm wondering, can you just stay with that feeling for a moment, without needing to do anything about it — what does it actually feel like to let it be there?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech
